problem_motivation.content: Hydrogen isotope retention in fusion-facing structural alloys is a major unresolved challenge.
problem_motivation.evidence_span: Hydrogen isotope retention in plasma-facing and structural alloys is a central materials challenge for deuterium-tritium fusion.

problem_motivation.content: Atomic-scale understanding of hydrogen isotope retention in irradiated materials is still needed.
problem_motivation.evidence_span: Understanding the atomic-scale mechanisms governing hydrogen isotope retention in irradiated structural materials therefore remains a central issue for fusion reactor development [5].

problem_motivation.content: The coupled effects of helium, segregation, and alloy chemistry on hydrogen retention are poorly understood.
problem_motivation.evidence_span: These coupled interactions between helium, radiation-induced segregation, and alloy chemistry may therefore critically influence hydrogen isotope retention in fusion environments, yet they remain poorly understood.

prior_approach.content: Cryogenic APT previously showed hydrogen localization at several defect sinks in martensitic steels.
prior_approach.evidence_span: Direct cryogenic atom probe tomography (APT) has provided nanoscale evidence that hydrogen localizes at dislocations, grain boundaries, and incoherent carbide interfaces in martensitic steels [7,8]

prior_approach.content: First-principles and kinetic Monte Carlo studies previously linked defect structure to hydrogen transport.
prior_approach.evidence_span: Complementary first-principles and kinetic Monte Carlo studies further demonstrate that the atomic structure of crystalline defects governs hydrogen transport by controlling local trapping energies and diffusion pathways [9].

prior_approach.content: TDS measurements previously identified temperature ranges for hydrogen release from different traps.
prior_approach.evidence_span: Complementary thermal desorption spectroscopy (TDS) measurements reveal that hydrogen trapped at dislocations is released primarily between ~100–300 °C, while trapping at grain boundaries and incoherent carbide interfaces corresponds to higher-temperature desorption peaks extending to ~300–350 °C.

prior_approach.content: Prior first-principles and thermodynamic studies quantified strong hydrogen binding at vacancies and Fe-He interfaces.
prior_approach.evidence_span: First-principles and thermodynamic studies further quantify the energetic hierarchy of these traps: vacancy and vacancy-cluster complexes in bcc Fe exhibit strong hydrogen binding energies of ~0.5–0.6 eV [10,11], while hydrogen binding at Fe–He interfaces ranges from ~0.59–0.92 eV depending on surface orientation and local helium density, although the binding strength generally decreases with increasing interfacial helium concentration [12].

prior_approach.content: Clowers et al. previously used triple-ion irradiation to separate effects of damage, helium, and hydrogen.
prior_approach.evidence_span: More recently, Clowers et al. [13,14] employed controlled triple-ion beam irradiations to decouple the respective roles of displacement damage, helium, and hydrogen under fusion-relevant conditions.

prior_approach.content: EELS previously found a core-shell cavity structure with helium inside and hydrogen near the surface.
prior_approach.evidence_span: Electron energy-loss spectroscopy (EELS) further revealed a distinct core–shell structure at 450 °C in Fe–Cr–W alloys, where helium preferentially occupies the cavity interior while hydrogen segregates near the cavity surface.

prior_approach.content: Prior MD simulations suggested transient hydrogen trapping at bubble interfaces with thermal instability at higher temperatures.
prior_approach.evidence_span: Complementary molecular dynamics (MD) simulations suggested that hydrogen can be transiently trapped at bubble interfaces, but becomes thermally unstable at elevated temperatures, with de-trapping occurring above ~127 °C [15,16].

prior_approach.content: Prior work suggested chromium may segregate to helium bubble interfaces under compression.
prior_approach.evidence_span: chromium in particular may preferentially segregate to helium bubble interfaces under compressive environments [22].

prior_approach.content: The study evaluated the chemical component of H adsorption using frozen-surface calculations
prior_approach.evidence_span: To capture this effect, we evaluated the chemical component of H adsorption using frozen-surface calculations [32]

prior_approach.content: Previous studies reported over-pressurized helium bubbles.
prior_approach.evidence_span: consistent with previous studies of over-pressurized helium bubbles [26]

prior_approach.evidence_span: [12] Z. J. Bergstrom, L. Yang, and B. D. Wirth, Hydrogen trapping energetics at BCC iron-helium interfaces, Journal of Nuclear Materials 572, 154064 (2022).

prior_approach.content: Prior work used MD to study the effect of helium bubbles on hydrogen retention in BCC iron.
prior_approach.evidence_span: [15] Z. Chen, L. Yang, X. Hu, B. D. Wirth, and M. Ye, MD simulation of the He bubble effect on H retention in BCC iron, Fusion Engineering and Design 180, 113184 (2022).

prior_approach.content: Prior work examined cavity evolution in BCC-Fe with coexisting hydrogen and helium under fusion conditions.
prior_approach.evidence_span: [16] J. Wang et al., Evolution of cavities in BCC-Fe with coexisting H and He under fusion environments, Acta Materialia 299, 121477 (2025).

prior_approach.content: Prior work developed a kinetic model for synergistic hydrogen and helium effects on helium bubble evolution in bcc iron.
prior_approach.evidence_span: [17] L. Shi, C. Chen, Q. Peng, and F. Gao, Synergistic effects of hydrogen and helium on He bubble evolution in bcc-iron: A kinetic model, Journal of Nuclear Materials 618, 156171 (2026).

prior_approach.content: Prior work investigated effects of alloying elements on hydrogen adsorption at low-indexed pure iron surfaces.

prior_approach.content: Prior work addressed Cr segregation at helium bubble surfaces in Fe.
prior_approach.evidence_span: [22] W. Hao and W. T. Geng, Understanding Cr segregation at the He bubble surface in Fe, J. Phys.: Condens. Matter 24, 095009 (2012).

prior_approach.content: Prior work studied hydrogen adsorption structures and energetics on iron surfaces at high coverage.

prior_approach.content: Prior work calculated hydrogen adsorption and diffusion energetics on Fe(110) from first principles.
prior_approach.evidence_span: [28] D. E. Jiang and E. A. Carter, Adsorption and diffusion energetics of hydrogen atoms on Fe(110) from first principles, Surface Science 547, 85 (2003).

prior_approach.content: Prior work on bimetallic surfaces considered strain and ligand effects on electronic and chemical properties.
prior_approach.evidence_span: [32] J. R. Kitchin, J. K. Nørskov, M. A. Barteau, and J. G. Chen, Role of Strain and Ligand Effects in the Modification of the Electronic and Chemical Properties of Bimetallic Surfaces, Phys. Rev. Lett. 93, 156801 (2004).

prior_limitation.content: Current atomistic models do not fully explain temperature-dependent hydrogen retention near helium cavities.
prior_limitation.evidence_span: These observations imply that hydrogen retention near helium cavities is strongly temperature dependent and cannot yet be fully explained by current atomistic models.

prior_limitation.content: Most atomistic studies considered pure Fe and did not explore alloying-element interactions with irradiation defects.
prior_limitation.evidence_span: However, most atomistic studies have focused on pure Fe, whereas fusion structural materials such as RAFM steels contain multiple alloying elements, and their interactions with irradiation-induced defect sinks, including voids and helium cavities, remain largely unexplored.

inspiration_source.content: The work is motivated by ion-beam irradiation experiments and first-principles calculations.
inspiration_source.evidence_span: Motivated by ion-beam irradiation experiments and first-principles calculations, we identify an irradiation- enabled mechanism whereby solute segregation to defect sinks enhances hydrogen isotope trapping.

inspiration_source.content: The computational investigation was guided by the experimental observations of segregated, hydrogen-enriched cavity interfaces
inspiration_source.evidence_span: Guided by these observations, we investigated H stability at Cr/Ta/W-enriched interfaces by determining electronic structures and chemical inhomogeneity, and by calculating H binding energy at both void and He cavity surfaces.

inspiration_source.content: Experimental and theoretical findings motivated the choice of two surface orientations for modeling
inspiration_source.evidence_span: Because experiments observed that helium bubble facets predominantly align with {100} planes in bcc Fe [25] and theoretical studies showed strong hydrogen adsorption on Fe (110) surfaces [26–28], two representative surface orientations, (100) and (110), were considered

inspiration_source.content: The study was guided by experimental observations of Cr, Ta, and W segregation at irradiation-induced cavities.
inspiration_source.evidence_span: Guided by experimental observations of Cr, Ta and W segregation at irradiation-induced cavities

causal_claim.content: Hydrogen co-injection increased cavity density and size relative to He-only irradiation.
causal_claim.evidence_span: Across multiple Fe-based alloys irradiated between 400 and 600 °C, co-injection of hydrogen with helium consistently increased both cavity density and cavity size compared with He-only irradiation.

causal_claim.content: Cr and Ta segregants increased hydrogen stability at cavities by strengthening binding and migration barriers, raising retention.
causal_claim.evidence_span: Density-functional theory shows that these segregants markedly increase H stability at cavities by strengthening binding energies and increasing migration barriers, leading to substantially higher attention.

causal_claim.content: Hydrogen trapping reduces fuel availability, raises costs, and imposes strict safety limits.
causal_claim.evidence_span: Trapped tritium directly reduces fuel availability, increases operational costs, and imposes strict safety limits on the in-vessel tritium inventory.

causal_claim.content: Hydrogen isotope trapping in components can increase required breeding ratio and lengthen doubling time.
causal_claim.evidence_span: fuel cycle modeling indicates that hydrogen isotope trapping in reactor components can significantly increase the required tritium breeding ratio (TBR) and prolong the tritium doubling time, thereby affecting the long-term sustainability of fusion power plants [2–4].

causal_claim.content: The observations indicate that helium cavities form chemically complex, solute- and hydrogen-enriched interfaces rather than pure Fe surfaces
causal_claim.evidence_span: Together, these observations demonstrate that helium cavities in irradiated RAFM steels form chemically complex interfaces enriched with both alloying elements and hydrogen, rather than idealized pure Fe surfaces.

causal_claim.content: Solute segregation enhances H binding, with the effect depending on orientation and coverage
causal_claim.evidence_span: On both Fe(100) and Fe(110) surfaces, segregation of Cr, Ta, and W generally enhances H binding relative to pure Fe. The magnitude of this enhancement depends strongly on surface orientation and solute coverage.

causal_claim.content: Higher helium density reduces H binding strength
causal_claim.evidence_span: A moderate helium density (He/V = 0.5) results in little change compared with the corresponding void surface (He/V = 0), while a higher helium density (He/V = 1) consistently reduces H binding strength.

causal_claim.content: Solute segregation increases the kinetic stability of interfacial hydrogen by raising escape barriers
causal_claim.evidence_span: In addition to enhancing thermodynamic stability, solute segregation also increases the kinetic stability of hydrogen at cavity interfaces. CI-NEB calculations (Fig. S2) show that alloying elements generally increase the migration barrier for H escape from the interface

causal_claim.evidence_span: Together, these results demonstrate that hydrogen retention at cavity interfaces is strongly influenced by both local composition and helium density

causal_claim.content: Ta and W enhance hydrogen stability on Fe(100) through strong d–H 1s hybridization
causal_claim.evidence_span: Ta and W atoms enhance hydrogen stability through strong hybridization between the solute d orbitals and the H 1s orbital.

causal_claim.content: Stronger local metal–H bonding promotes enhanced hydrogen stability at the cavity interface

causal_claim.content: Increasing solute coverage changes hydrogen stability by modifying bonding geometry and electronic environment
causal_claim.evidence_span: Increasing solute coverage further modifies H stability by altering both the local bonding geometry and the electronic environment.

causal_claim.content: Charge transfer is an effective descriptor of solute-enhanced hydrogen stabilization on the (100) surface
causal_claim.evidence_span: These results demonstrate that charge transfer serves as an effective descriptor of solute-enhanced hydrogen stabilization on the (100) surface.

causal_claim.content: Hydrogen stability is influenced not only by local bonding and charge transfer but also by the collective electronic structure of the surface
causal_claim.evidence_span: These observations indicate that, in addition to local bonding and charge transfer, H stability is also influenced by the collective electronic structure of the surface.

causal_claim.evidence_span: Consistent with this picture, W significantly lowers the d-band center on Fe(110) surface, reducing the chemical contribution to H binding despite the presence of strong local W–H interactions.

causal_claim.content: A Cr monolayer shifts the d-band center toward the Fermi level and promotes stronger H adsorption.

causal_claim.content: Helium accumulation modifies hydrogen stability through coupled mechanical and electronic perturbations at the cavity interface.

causal_claim.content: Stronger trapping and higher migration barriers at solute-enriched interfaces enhance hydrogen retention thermodynamically and kinetically.

mechanism_principle.content: Solutes can alter hydrogen adsorption and defect energetics via electronic and chemical effects.
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: Solutes can modify hydrogen adsorption and defect energetics through electronic and chemical effects [19–21]

mechanism_principle.content: The effect is attributed to solute-tuned electronic structure, with Ta enhancing H 1s-metal d hybridization and Cr shifting the d-band to favor bonding.
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: The effect originates from solute-tuned electronic structure: Ta promotes strong H 1s–metal d orbital hybridization, whereas Cr shifts the surface d-band toward a more favorable bonding configuration.

mechanism_principle.content: Helium clusters were modeled with selected He/V ratios because helium assemblies are liquid-like and density-governed
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: Helium cavities were modeled by introducing ordered helium clusters above Fe surfaces, with densities corresponding to He-to- vacancy (He/V) ratios of 0.5 and 1, reflecting the liquid-like, density-governed nature of helium assemblies [22,29].

mechanism_principle.content: Higher migration barriers are explained by the corresponding increase in H binding energy
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: CI-NEB calculations (Fig. S2) show that alloying elements generally increase the migration barrier for H escape from the interface, consistent with the corresponding increase in H binding energy.

mechanism_principle.content: The lower migration barrier at higher helium density is attributed to over-pressurized helium destabilizing interfacial hydrogen
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: reflecting the destabilizing effect of over-pressurized helium on interfacial hydrogen.

mechanism_principle.content: The higher migration barrier is consistent with stronger hydrogen binding energy
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: consistent with the corresponding increase in H binding energy

mechanism_principle.content: Over-pressurized helium destabilizes interfacial hydrogen, explaining the lower migration barrier

mechanism_principle.content: Local chemical identity of alloying elements modifies metal–H bonding and contributes to hydrogen stability
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: The first contribution arises from the local chemical identity of the alloying elements, which directly modifies metal– H bonding.

mechanism_principle.content: The charge-density pattern indicates enhanced charge transfer to hydrogen
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: indicating enhanced charge transfer to H

mechanism_principle.content: An upward shift of the surface d-band center favors H adsorption by enhancing bonding-state occupation while limiting antibonding occupation
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: Within the d- band framework, an upward shift of the surface d-band center favors H adsorption by enhancing bonding-state occupation while keeping antibonding

mechanism_principle.content: An upward d-band-center shift strengthens H adsorption by filling bonding states while keeping antibonding states less occupied.
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: Within the d- band framework, an upward shift of the surface d-band center favors H adsorption by enhancing bonding-state occupation while keeping antibonding states less occupied.

mechanism_principle.content: A downward d-band-center shift weakens chemical adsorption by increasing antibonding occupation.
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: In contrast, a downward shift increases antibonding-state occupation and weakens the chemical contribution to H adsorption.

mechanism_principle.content: Compression of the H localization basin reflects reduced charge transfer from neighboring metal atoms to H.
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: reflecting a reduced ability of neighboring metal atoms to transfer charge to H.

mechanism_principle.content: Enhanced hydrogen stability comes from stronger local metal-H hybridization, greater charge transfer to H, and solute-driven d-band modification increasing the chemical driving force for adsorption.
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: Electronic- structure analysis reveals that the enhanced stability originates from the combined effects of strengthened local metal–H hybridization, increased charge transfer to hydrogen, and solute-induced modification of the surface d-band structure, which collectively increase the intrinsic chemical driving force for H adsorption.

hypothesis_statement.content: The study proposes that composition and chemical inhomogeneity control hydrogen interactions with cavities.
hypothesis_statement.evidence_span: To address these puzzles, we combine experiments and computer simulations to study how composition and chemical inhomogeneity affect hydrogen interactions with cavities.

hypothesis_statement.content: The paper proposes an irradiation-enabled mechanism in which solute segregation to defect sinks enhances hydrogen trapping.
hypothesis_statement.evidence_span: we identify an irradiation- enabled mechanism whereby solute segregation to defect sinks enhances hydrogen isotope trapping.

hypothesis_statement.content: The study proposes an atomistic framework linking solute segregation to hydrogen retention at helium cavities
hypothesis_statement.evidence_span: By examining the effects of helium density and solute coverage on hydrogen stability and migration barriers, this study establishes an atomistic framework linking solute segregation with hydrogen retention at helium cavities.

evidence_result.content: Reported de-trapping enthalpy agreed with TDS-measured trapping energies and temperatures.

prior_approach.content: Prior EELS measurements in Fe–Cr–W alloys found a core–shell cavity structure at 450 °C, with helium concentrated in the cavity interior and hydrogen segregated near the cavity surface.
evidence_spans: Electron energy-loss spectroscopy (EELS) further revealed a distinct core–shell structure at 450 °C in Fe–Cr–W alloys, where helium preferentially occupies the cavity interior while hydrogen segregates near the cavity surface.

prior_approach.content: Prior atomistic studies of H at He bubbles/interfaces indicated that hydrogen can be retained or trapped at Fe–He bubble interfaces/cavities, but this trapping may be transient and thermally unstable at elevated temperature, with MD reporting de-trapping above ~127 °C; related work also examined He-bubble effects on H retention, cavity evolution with coexisting H and He, and kinetic modeling of their synergistic effects in bcc Fe.
evidence_spans: Complementary molecular dynamics (MD) simulations suggested that hydrogen can be transiently trapped at bubble interfaces, but becomes thermally unstable at elevated temperatures, with de-trapping occurring above ~127 °C [15,16].
[15] Z. Chen, L. Yang, X. Hu, B. D. Wirth, and M. Ye, MD simulation of the He bubble effect on H retention in BCC iron, Fusion Engineering and Design 180, 113184 (2022).
[16] J. Wang et al., Evolution of cavities in BCC-Fe with coexisting H and He under fusion environments, Acta Materialia 299, 121477 (2025).
[17] L. Shi, C. Chen, Q. Peng, and F. Gao, Synergistic effects of hydrogen and helium on He bubble evolution in bcc-iron: A kinetic model, Journal of Nuclear Materials 618, 156171 (2026).

prior_approach.content: Previous studies reported over-pressurized helium bubbles.
evidence_spans: consistent with previous studies of over-pressurized helium bubbles [26]

prior_approach.content: Prior work suggested that chromium can segregate to helium bubble interfaces/surfaces in Fe, particularly under compressive conditions.
evidence_spans: chromium in particular may preferentially segregate to helium bubble interfaces under compressive environments [22].
[22] W. Hao and W. T. Geng, Understanding Cr segregation at the He bubble surface in Fe, J. Phys.: Condens. Matter 24, 095009 (2012).

prior_approach.content: Prior surface-science studies examined hydrogen adsorption on iron, including first-principles adsorption and diffusion on Fe(110), adsorption structures and energetics at high coverage, and effects of alloying elements on hydrogen adsorption at low-index iron surfaces.
evidence_spans: [20] Z. Xu, L. Cheng, K. Xia, L. Cheng, C. Hu, X. Liu, R. Wang, F. Zheng, and K. Wu, Effects of alloying elements on hydrogen adsorption behaviors at low- indexed surfaces of pure iron, International Journal of Hydrogen Energy 140, 653 (2025).
[27] T. Wang, S. Wang, Q. Luo, Y.-W. Li, J. Wang, M. Beller, and H. Jiao, Hydrogen Adsorption Structures and Energetics on Iron Surfaces at High Coverage, J. Phys. Chem. C 118, 4181 (2014).
[28] D. E. Jiang and E. A. Carter, Adsorption and diffusion energetics of hydrogen atoms on Fe(110) from first principles, Surface Science 547, 85 (2003).

prior_approach.content: Prior methodological work on bimetallic surfaces analyzed how strain and ligand effects modify electronic structure and chemical properties; the present study draws on this framework via frozen-surface calculations to isolate the chemical component of H adsorption.
evidence_spans: To capture this effect, we evaluated the chemical component of H adsorption using frozen-surface calculations [32]

[32] J. R. Kitchin, J. K. Nørskov, M. A. Barteau, and J. G. Chen, Role of Strain and Ligand Effects in the Modification of the Electronic and Chemical Properties of Bimetallic Surfaces, Phys. Rev. Lett. 93, 156801 (2004).

prior_limitation.content: Current atomistic models do not fully explain the strongly temperature-dependent hydrogen retention near helium cavities.
evidence_spans: These observations imply that hydrogen retention near helium cavities is strongly temperature dependent and cannot yet be fully explained by current atomistic models.

prior_limitation.content: Most atomistic studies have focused on pure Fe and have largely not explored how alloying elements in fusion structural materials interact with irradiation-induced defect sinks such as voids and helium cavities.
evidence_spans: However, most atomistic studies have focused on pure Fe, whereas fusion structural materials such as RAFM steels contain multiple alloying elements, and their interactions with irradiation-induced defect sinks, including voids and helium cavities, remain largely unexplored.

inspiration_source.content: The study was motivated and guided by ion-beam irradiation experiments and associated observations of irradiation-induced cavities with Cr/Ta/W segregation and hydrogen-enriched interfaces, which in turn led the authors to investigate H stability/trapping at Cr/Ta/W-enriched interfaces.
evidence_spans: Motivated by ion-beam irradiation experiments and first-principles calculations, we identify an irradiation- enabled mechanism whereby solute segregation to defect sinks enhances hydrogen isotope trapping.

Guided by these observations, we investigated H stability at Cr/Ta/W-enriched interfaces by determining electronic structures and chemical inhomogeneity, and by calculating H binding energy at both void and He cavity surfaces.
Guided by experimental observations of Cr, Ta and W segregation at irradiation-induced cavities

inspiration_source.content: The modeling choice of surface orientations was inspired by prior experimental and theoretical findings: experiments showed helium bubble facets mainly align with {100} planes in bcc Fe, while theoretical studies showed strong hydrogen adsorption on Fe(110), motivating use of (100) and (110) surfaces.
evidence_spans: Because experiments observed that helium bubble facets predominantly align with {100} planes in bcc Fe [25] and theoretical studies showed strong hydrogen adsorption on Fe (110) surfaces [26–28], two representative surface orientations, (100) and (110), were considered

causal_claim.content: Hydrogen co-injection increased cavity density and size relative to He-only irradiation.
evidence_spans: Across multiple Fe-based alloys irradiated between 400 and 600 °C, co-injection of hydrogen with helium consistently increased both cavity density and cavity size compared with He-only irradiation.

causal_claim.content: Hydrogen isotope trapping in reactor components reduces fuel availability, increases operational costs and safety constraints, and can increase the required tritium breeding ratio and prolong tritium doubling time.
evidence_spans: Trapped tritium directly reduces fuel availability, increases operational costs, and imposes strict safety limits on the in-vessel tritium inventory.

fuel cycle modeling indicates that hydrogen isotope trapping in reactor components can significantly increase the required tritium breeding ratio (TBR) and prolong the tritium doubling time, thereby affecting the long-term sustainability of fusion power plants [2–4].

causal_claim.content: Helium cavities in irradiated RAFM steels form chemically complex, solute- and hydrogen-enriched interfaces rather than idealized pure Fe surfaces.
evidence_spans: Together, these observations demonstrate that helium cavities in irradiated RAFM steels form chemically complex interfaces enriched with both alloying elements and hydrogen, rather than idealized pure Fe surfaces.

causal_claim.content: Hydrogen retention at cavity interfaces depends strongly on local composition, solute coverage/orientation, and helium density: solute segregation generally enhances H binding and kinetic stability by increasing binding energies and raising escape barriers, whereas high helium density weakens H binding and lowers migration barriers.
evidence_spans: Together, these results demonstrate that hydrogen retention at cavity interfaces is strongly influenced by both local composition and helium density

On both Fe(100) and Fe(110) surfaces, segregation of Cr, Ta, and W generally enhances H binding relative to pure Fe. The magnitude of this enhancement depends strongly on surface orientation and solute coverage.

Density-functional theory shows that these segregants markedly increase H stability at cavities by strengthening binding energies and increasing migration barriers, leading to substantially higher attention.

In addition to enhancing thermodynamic stability, solute segregation also increases the kinetic stability of hydrogen at cavity interfaces. CI-NEB calculations (Fig. S2) show that alloying elements generally increase the migration barrier for H escape from the interface)

A moderate helium density (He/V = 0.5) results in little change compared with the corresponding void surface (He/V = 0), while a higher helium density (He/V = 1) consistently reduces H binding strength.
Increasing helium density tends to reduce the migration barrier, particularly for pure Fe and Cr-decorated surfaces
thereby enhancing hydrogen retention both thermodynamically and kinetically.
Increasing solute coverage further modifies H stability by altering both the local bonding geometry and the electronic environment.

causal_claim.content: Ta remains effective in stabilizing hydrogen even under high-helium conditions, helping explain experimentally observed high-temperature hydrogen retention at Cr- and Ta-segregated void and helium-cavity surfaces.
evidence_spans: indicating that Ta remains effective in stabilizing hydrogen even under high-He conditions
explaining the experimentally observation of high-temperature hydrogen retention at both void and helium-cavity surfaces.

causal_claim.content: Stronger local metal-H bonding promotes enhanced hydrogen stability at cavity interfaces; on Fe(100), Ta and W enhance H stability through strong d-H 1s hybridization.
evidence_spans: These results indicate that stronger local metal–H bonding promotes enhanced hydrogen stability at the cavity interface.
Ta and W atoms enhance hydrogen stability through strong hybridization between the solute d orbitals and the H 1s orbital.

causal_claim.content: Charge transfer and the collective electronic structure of the surface govern solute-enhanced hydrogen stabilization; solute-induced redistribution of surface d states controls the intrinsic chemical driving force for H adsorption.
evidence_spans: These results demonstrate that charge transfer serves as an effective descriptor of solute-enhanced hydrogen stabilization on the (100) surface.
These observations indicate that, in addition to local bonding and charge transfer, H stability is also influenced by the collective electronic structure of the surface.
demonstrating that solute-induced redistribution of surface d states controls the intrinsic chemical driving force for H adsorption.

causal_claim.content: Surface-specific d-band shifts caused by segregants alter H adsorption: on Fe(110), W lowers the d-band center and reduces the chemical contribution to H binding despite strong local W-H interactions, whereas a Cr monolayer shifts the d-band center toward the Fermi level and promotes stronger H adsorption.
evidence_spans: Consistent with this picture, W significantly lowers the d-band center on Fe(110) surface, reducing the chemical contribution to H binding despite the presence of strong local W–H interactions.
By contrast, a Cr monolayer shifts the surface d-band center toward the Fermi level, thereby promoting stronger H adsorption.

causal_claim.content: Helium accumulation weakens hydrogen trapping and destabilizes H at cavity interfaces through coupled mechanical and electronic effects associated with helium-induced compression, which reduces charge transfer and lowers H binding energies; increasing helium density also lowers migration barriers.
evidence_spans: Helium accumulation further modifies hydrogen stability through coupled mechanical and electronic perturbations at the cavity interface.
Consequently, the reduced charge transfer provides an electronic origin for the lower H binding energies observed at over-pressurized helium cavities.
Together, these results demonstrate that helium weakens hydrogen trapping through coupled mechanical and electronic effects associated with helium-induced compression.

In contrast, helium accumulation introduces a destabilizing effect through helium-induced compression, which reduces charge transfer and weakens hydrogen stabilization at over-pressurized cavity interfaces.
Increasing helium density tends to reduce the migration barrier, particularly for pure Fe and Cr-decorated surfaces

mechanism_principle.content: Solutes/alloying elements modify hydrogen adsorption, defect energetics, and interfacial H stability through local chemical and electronic effects: they change metal–H bonding via strengthened local metal–H hybridization, increased charge transfer to H, and solute-tuned surface electronic structure.
evidence_spans: Solutes can modify hydrogen adsorption and defect energetics through electronic and chemical effects [19–21]
The first contribution arises from the local chemical identity of the alloying elements, which directly modifies metal– H bonding.

Electronic- structure analysis reveals that the enhanced stability originates from the combined effects of strengthened local metal–H hybridization, increased charge transfer to hydrogen, and solute-induced modification of the surface d-band structure, which collectively increase the intrinsic chemical driving force for H adsorption.
indicating enhanced charge transfer to H

mechanism_principle.content: Specific solute electronic-structure changes explain stronger H bonding: Ta enhances H 1s–metal d hybridization, while Cr shifts the surface d-band toward a more favorable bonding configuration.
evidence_spans: The effect originates from solute-tuned electronic structure: Ta promotes strong H 1s–metal d orbital hybridization, whereas Cr shifts the surface d-band toward a more favorable bonding configuration.

mechanism_principle.content: Within the d-band framework, an upward shift of the surface d-band center strengthens/favors H adsorption by increasing bonding-state occupation while keeping antibonding states less occupied, whereas a downward shift weakens adsorption by increasing antibonding occupation.
evidence_spans: Within the d- band framework, an upward shift of the surface d-band center favors H adsorption by enhancing bonding-state occupation while keeping antibonding
Within the d- band framework, an upward shift of the surface d-band center favors H adsorption by enhancing bonding-state occupation while keeping antibonding states less occupied.
In contrast, a downward shift increases antibonding-state occupation and weakens the chemical contribution to H adsorption.

mechanism_principle.content: Charge-density/localization features are interpreted mechanistically in terms of charge transfer: enhanced charge-density around H indicates increased charge transfer to H, while compression of the H localization basin indicates reduced charge transfer from neighboring metal atoms to H.
evidence_spans: indicating enhanced charge transfer to H
reflecting a reduced ability of neighboring metal atoms to transfer charge to H.

mechanism_principle.content: Alloying elements generally raise the migration barrier for H escape from the interface because they increase H binding energy; conversely, at higher helium density the lower migration barrier is attributed to over-pressurized helium destabilizing interfacial hydrogen.
evidence_spans: CI-NEB calculations (Fig. S2) show that alloying elements generally increase the migration barrier for H escape from the interface, consistent with the corresponding increase in H binding energy.
consistent with the corresponding increase in H binding energy

mechanism_principle.content: Helium cavities were modeled using selected He/V ratios because helium assemblies are treated as liquid-like and governed by density.
evidence_spans: Helium cavities were modeled by introducing ordered helium clusters above Fe surfaces, with densities corresponding to He-to- vacancy (He/V) ratios of 0.5 and 1, reflecting the liquid-like, density-governed nature of helium assemblies [22,29].

hypothesis_statement.content: The study hypothesizes that composition and chemical inhomogeneity—specifically irradiation-induced solute segregation to defect sinks and helium cavities—control hydrogen interactions, trapping, and retention at cavities by enhancing hydrogen isotope trapping and affecting hydrogen stability and migration barriers.
evidence_spans: To address these puzzles, we combine experiments and computer simulations to study how composition and chemical inhomogeneity affect hydrogen interactions with cavities.
we identify an irradiation- enabled mechanism whereby solute segregation to defect sinks enhances hydrogen isotope trapping.

By examining the effects of helium density and solute coverage on hydrogen stability and migration barriers, this study establishes an atomistic framework linking solute segregation with hydrogen retention at helium cavities.

evidence_result.content: The calculated de-trapping enthalpy (~0.703 eV) agrees with TDS-measured hydrogen/deuterium trapping energies (~0.75 eV) and corresponding de-trapping temperatures (~227–327 °C) in He-implanted Fe.
evidence_spans: The calculated de- trapping enthalpy is ~0.703 eV [17], in good agreement with thermal desorption spectroscopy (TDS) measurements in He-implanted Fe that reported hydrogen/deuterium trapping energies of 0.75 eV, corresponding to de-trapping temperatures near 227– 327 °C [18].

evidence_result.content: Triple-ion irradiation experiments on F82H, including EDS mapping, found pronounced segregation of Cr and Ta to cavity surfaces throughout the depth-dependent damage region, while W does not show pronounced segregation and remains broadly distributed around the cavity region.
evidence_spans: Triple-ion irradiation of reduced activation ferritic–martensitic steel F82H reveals pronounced segregation of Cr and Ta to cavity surfaces.

Each set of images reveals clear segregation of chromium and tantalum at cavity surfaces throughout the depth-dependent damage region, while tungsten does not exhibit pronounced segregation but remains broadly distributed around the cavity region.

evidence_result.content: Hydrogen enrichment at He cavity surfaces was experimentally observed previously as a pronounced H-rich shell surrounding the cavity interface.
evidence_spans: In the same samples, hydrogen enrichment at He cavity surfaces was also experimentally observed and reported in our previous study [23], where a pronounced H-rich shell was found to surround the cavity interface.

evidence_result.content: First-principles calculations show that solute-enriched cavity interfaces trap hydrogen more strongly and have higher migration barriers than pure Fe surfaces; specifically, Cr, Ta, and W generally enhance H binding relative to pure Fe, and alloying elements generally increase the migration barrier for H escape from the interface.
evidence_spans: first- principles calculations show that solute-enriched interfaces exhibit stronger hydrogen trapping and higher migration barriers than pure Fe surfaces
On both Fe(100) and Fe(110) surfaces, segregation of Cr, Ta, and W generally enhances H binding relative to pure Fe.

evidence_result.content: The strongest alloying effects are orientation- and coverage-dependent: on Fe(100), Ta gives the largest increase in H binding energy and the largest migration-barrier enhancement; on Fe(110), Cr becomes most favorable at higher H coverages and has the stronger barrier-enhancing effect, while W traps H most strongly at intermediate coverage but at full monolayer coverage its binding drops to pure-Fe-like or lower, with 1 ML W on Fe(110) reducing overall H binding below pure Fe.
evidence_spans: On Fe(100), Ta produces the largest increase in H binding energy, whereas on Fe(110), Cr becomes increasingly favorable at higher coverages.
On the Fe(100) surface, Ta produces the largest barrier enhancement, whereas Cr has a stronger effect on Fe(110).

Tungsten exhibits maximum H trapping at intermediate coverages, whereas full monolayer coverage reduces the H binding energy to values comparable to or lower than those of pure Fe.

evidence_result.content: Helium-density effects on H trapping are nonmonotonic: moderate helium density (He/V = 0.5) changes H binding little relative to a void surface, whereas high helium density (He/V = 1) reduces H binding strength; despite this, Cr- and Ta-segregated interfaces remain effective hydrogen traps over a wide range of helium densities, and migration barriers on Ta-decorated surfaces are comparatively insensitive to helium accumulation.
evidence_spans: A moderate helium density (He/V = 0.5) results in little change compared with the corresponding void surface (He/V = 0), while a higher helium density (He/V = 1) consistently reduces H binding strength.

evidence_result.content: Electronic-structure analyses indicate stronger local metal–H bonding for Ta and W than for Fe: COHP shows Ta–H and W–H bonds have larger bonding contributions than Fe–H, integrated COHP correlates positively with H binding energy, and supplementary COHP indicates W and Ta continue to form strong local metal–H bonds on Fe(110).
evidence_spans: Ta–H and W–H bonds exhibit substantially larger bonding contributions than Fe–H.
the integrated crystal orbital Hamilton population (-ICOHP), which quantifies the overall bond strength, correlates positively with the H binding energy

evidence_result.content: At the atomic scale, on pure Fe(100) H occupies a symmetric hollow site coordinated by Fe atoms, whereas with a Ta monolayer H is stabilized near surface Ta atoms.
evidence_spans: On the pure Fe(100) surface, H occupies a symmetric hollow site (HS) coordinated by neighboring Fe atoms.
when a Ta monolayer is present at the interface, H becomes stabilized near the surface Ta atoms

evidence_result.content: Charge analyses show electron accumulation around adsorbed H and depletion around nearby metal atoms; for (100) interfaces, greater charge transfer to H correlates positively with stronger H binding, whereas on Fe(110) this relationship is weaker, especially for Ta- and W-decorated surfaces.
evidence_spans: The corresponding charge-density-difference maps reveal substantial electron accumulation around the adsorbed H, together with charge depletion around neighboring metal atoms
Quantitative Bader analysis further confirms this trend [31], showing a positive correlation between the charge transferred to H and the H binding energy for (100) interfaces (Fig. 3c).
As shown in Fig. 3d, the dependence of H binding energy on charge transfer becomes weaker for Fe(110) interfaces, particularly for Ta and W-decorated surfaces.

evidence_result.content: Increasing helium density generates a strong compressive strain field near the cavity surface, similarly for both Fe(100) and Fe(110), indicating the effect depends mainly on the local helium environment rather than specific surface geometry; correspondingly, ELF maps show compression of the H localization basin and Bader analysis shows reduced H charge gain at He/V = 1 versus helium-free interfaces.
evidence_spans: As shown in Fig. 3f for Fe(100) and Fig. S4 for Fe(110), increasing helium density generates a strong compressive strain field near the cavity surface
A similar response is observed for both surface orientations, indicating that the effect originates primarily from the local helium environment rather than the specific surface geometry.
The corresponding electron localization function (ELF) maps reveal a pronounced compression of the H localization basin in the presence of helium
Quantitative Bader analysis further supports this interpretation, showing a reduced H charge gain at He/V = 1 compared with the helium-free interfaces
